questions.question: Why must large food molecules like proteins and fats be broken down during digestion?
options: To turn them into energy before they enter the bloodstream
To convert them into smaller molecules that can be absorbed by the body
To allow them to pass directly through the windpipe
To help them mix with water in the stomach

questions.question: Once nutrients are absorbed into the blood, how do they reach the cells that need them?
options: They are stored in the liver and transported only when sleeping
They travel through the nervous system to the brain
They are transported around the body by the blood circulatory system
They move through air pockets in the skeletal system

questions.question: By what process do some small nutrient molecules move from the digestive system into the blood?
options: Active muscular pumping
Osmosis of proteins
Diffusion
Filtration by gravity

questions.question: Which feature of the small intestine lining is an adaptation that increases the amount of nutrient absorption?
options: Highly folded surface area with tiny projections called villi
A thick, smooth layer of impermeable fat
A dry surface that prevents water from entering
A system of muscular valves that block blood flow

questions.question: What is a bacterium?
options: A multicellular fungus that feeds on waste
A microscopic virus that cannot replicate on its own
A tiny particle made only of protein strands
A microorganism made of a single living cell

questions.question: Which of the following statements about bacteria is correct?
options: All bacteria cause disease in humans.
Bacteria are not living organisms because they lack cells.
Many bacteria are harmless and some are actually helpful.
Helpful bacteria only exist outside the human body.

questions.question: Where do helpful bacteria that assist in human digestion primarily live?
options: Inside the human digestive system
Inside the lungs and windpipe
In the acid-filled chamber of the heart
On the dry outer surface of our nails

questions.question: How do helpful bacteria in our digestive system assist in digesting foods that we cannot digest ourselves?
options: They physically chew the food using microscopic teeth.
They release enzymes that break down these foods.
They heat up the stomach to dissolve the food.
They absorb the food whole and carry it to the liver.

questions.question: How do helpful bacteria protect us from harmful pathogens that enter our digestive system?
options: By producing white blood cells to attack them
By competing against them for resources and space
By raising our body temperature to cause a fever
By physically blocking the entrance to the stomach

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a digestion type with its description and location?
options: Mechanical digestion involves enzymes and occurs only in the large intestine.
Chemical digestion involves physically breaking food into smaller pieces in the stomach only.
Mechanical digestion physically breaks down food (like chewing in the mouth), while chemical digestion uses chemicals/enzymes to break bonds.
Chemical digestion physically grinds food and occurs only in the esophagus.

questions.question: What are the three main types of large nutrient molecules that make up our food?
options: Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats
Vitamins, minerals, and water only
Sugars, starches, and fiber only
Enzymes, acids, and hormones

questions.question: What is the primary role of enzymes during chemical digestion?
options: They act as biological catalysts to speed up the breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
They slow down digestion so that nutrients are absorbed over several days.
They act as structural blocks to build muscle tissue directly in the stomach.
They line the esophagus to lubricate the passage of dry food.

questions.question: According to how enzymes break down nutrients, which of the following is correct?
options: Proteins are digested into fatty acids and glycerol.
Fats are digested into starch and simple sugars.
Proteins are digested into amino acids, and fats are digested into fatty acids and glycerol.
Carbohydrates are digested into amino acids.

questions.question: Which reagent is commonly used to test for the presence of the large carbohydrate starch in food?
options: Biuret solution
Iodine solution
Benedict's solution
Ethanol emulsion

questions.question: Which chemical reagent and conditions are used to test for smaller sugar molecules resulting from the breakdown of starch?
options: Cold iodine solution
Benedict's solution heated in a water bath
Biuret reagent at room temperature
Acidic ethanol mixed with cold water

questions.question: A student adds Biuret reagent to a food sample, and the color changes from blue to purple. What does this qualitative result indicate?
options: The food sample contains a high concentration of starch.
The food sample contains protein.
The food sample contains simple sugars.
The food sample contains lipids/fats.

questions.question: What is the correct order of major organs that food passes through after entering the mouth?
options: Mouth -> Stomach -> Esophagus -> Large Intestine -> Small Intestine
Mouth -> Esophagus -> Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Large Intestine
Mouth -> Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Esophagus -> Large Intestine
Mouth -> Esophagus -> Large Intestine -> Small Intestine -> Stomach

questions.question: How is the stomach adapted to perform its function in the digestive system?
options: It has a thin, dry lining that absorbs gases directly into the blood.
It contains muscular walls to churn food and glands that release acid and digestive enzymes.
It is completely smooth to allow food to slide quickly into the large intestine.
It contains villi to absorb most of the digested fats.

questions.question: What happens to food material that cannot be digested as it passes through the digestive tract?
options: It is completely dissolved by stomach acid and exhaled as carbon dioxide.
It is converted into white blood cells by the liver.
It is stored permanently in the small intestine.
It is passed out of the body as faeces.
